title: Lumbini found
hook: Ashoka's pillar was found at Lumbini, marking the birthplace

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vietnam, where Mahayana and Theravada share one country and Chan becomes Thien. Your line was two streams meet. Where did two ways make room for each other near you? Today, back to the very beginning. Day eight hundred ninety-three.

A dig on the flat, hot plain of southern Nepal, close to the Indian border. Workers clear away earth around a stone column standing half buried near a small shrine. The pillar is broken at the top, and it's plain, no statue, no carving to speak of. But low down on the shaft there's writing, in an old script. Someone copies the letters out, line by line. And the inscription turns out to say, more or less: this is the place. Here the Buddha was born. After all the travels of the last weeks, from Sri Lanka to Java, today we go back to the very start of the story. Lumbini, found.
screen: `A HALF-BURIED PILLAR IN NEPAL.` → `WRITING LOW ON THE SHAFT.` → `HERE THE BUDDHA WAS BORN.`

segments.voice: First, a place the texts remember. In the Sutta Nipata, a sage named Asita hears that a child has been born who will one day awaken, born in a village of the Sakyans, in the Lumbini country. In the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the Buddha himself names the place of his birth as one of the places a faithful follower might visit and be moved. So the name was never lost from the scriptures. Second, a place that slipped out of sight. As Buddhism faded in India, the garden itself was overgrown, and where exactly it lay became a question rather than a fact. Third, a king's stone answers it. The pillar that came out of the ground was set up by Ashoka, the emperor we met earlier this year. His inscription says, in plain words, that twenty years after he was anointed, the king came here himself and worshiped, because here the Buddha, the sage of the Sakyas, was born. He had a stone pillar raised, and he made the village of Lumbini free of tax, paying only an eighth share of its harvest. Fourth, why this matters. A holy place can rest on memory alone. This one also has a king's own words, carved at the spot. Pilgrims had a name; now they had a place to stand. Today Lumbini has gardens, a pool, temples built by Buddhists from different countries, and the old pillar, still standing, still saying the same thing. A sentence in stone, waiting in the ground until someone could read it.
screen: `THE TEXTS REMEMBER LUMBINI.` · `THE GARDEN SLIPS OUT OF SIGHT.` · `ASHOKA'S PILLAR: HERE HE WAS BORN.` · `A NAME BECOMES A PLACE TO STAND.` · then, large: `THE BIRTHPLACE FOUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find Lumbini on a map. If you have a phone or a map nearby, look for it in southern Nepal, just north of the border with India. If not, picture the flat green plain, the pool, the old pillar in the sun. Then sit with this for the rest of the time: one birth, in a garden, on a journey. Everything we've followed across these weeks, the stupas, the chronicles, the golden towers, began with a child born here. Breathe with that. The bell holds the time.
Lumbini found. The garden of the Buddha's birth, named in the scriptures, then located again by Ashoka's pillar and its words: here he was born. Today's word.
Your line: the birthplace found. Today, think of where someone you love was born, and if you can, ask them about it. Day eight hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Buddhists from different countries travel to Lumbini in Nepal as pilgrims, visiting the garden, the pool, the temple at the birth site and Ashoka's pillar, and some walk on to the other places named in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta.

notes: All paraphrased; nothing quoted. The index hook's year (1896) is left out of the hook field and the voice under the claims rule, since none of the cited texts give it. Discoverers (Führer, Khadga Shamsher Rana) not named for the same reason.

Inscription paraphrase: twenty years after his anointing, came himself and worshiped, 'here the Buddha Shakyamuni was born', stone pillar set up, village made tax-free and paying an eighth share. Confirm against Hultzsch.
Hook details (broken top, near a small shrine, half buried) follow the usual account of the find; confirm.
'As Buddhism faded in India, the garden itself was overgrown': general; confirm wording.
'Ashoka, the emperor we met earlier this year' assumes the Ashoka days earlier in year 3; confirm.
Sutta Nipata 683: Asita hears from the devas that the Bodhisatta is born in the Sakyans' village, in the Lumbini country. Confirm.
The pillar is described as 'plain, no statue': the capital is lost; confirm.

Audit: practice called the birth 'ordinary'; the traditional accounts describe it as marvelous, so the narrator's adjective was cut. Otherwise checked against the Lumbini inscription and Sn 683; no change.
